title: The 7 Habits of Highly Ineffective Leaders
author: The Good Boss
summary: An inverted frame on leadership advice: the author argues that after two decades in tech and leadership roles, the clearest pattern across failed projects and derailed careers is not missing virtues but recurring bad habits. Seven of them, each subtle, each individually defensible in the moment, each quietly corrosive over time. The piece reads like a diagnostic rather than a lecture, and its usefulness is in the fact that every leader will recognize at least one. The taxonomy is: confusing control with leadership (the fear response that looks like rigor), always having the final word (the silencing effect on creativity and dissent), rewarding outcomes but not effort (which trains a team against honest risk-taking), avoiding hard conversations (kindness as long-term harm), chasing every shiny object (making everything a priority, which means nothing is), hiding behind busyness (the calendar as shield from the actual work of coaching), and never looking in the mirror (the habit that blocks every other habit from improving). The corrective moves the author offers are the natural mirrors of each habit: delegate real ownership, ask more questions than you answer, reward smart risks even when they fail, be direct and kind, protect the team's focus, make time for the people, and diagnose problems by looking inward first. For a school leader or instructional coach, the habits translate directly. Control-by-approval, the last-word meeting, the never-delivered hard conversation, and the shield of busyness show up in education settings as reliably as in tech, and the piece is useful as a self-audit prompt rather than a management manifesto.
points: Confusing control with leadership,micromanagement and endless approvals teach teams to stop thinking for themselves and wait to be told.
Rewarding outcomes but punishing honest risk-taking trains teams against experimentation and creates a culture where failure is simply not an option.
Avoiding hard conversations under the guise of kindness creates long-term damage through missed feedback moments that compound into broken trust.
Everything cannot be a priority, because when everything is urgent nothing matters,chaotic priorities exhaust teams and obscure the actual finish line.
Busyness is not leadership; it is avoidance, and the meetings that matter most (1:1s, coaching, feedback) are the first to disappear into the shield of an overfilled calendar.
quotes: Micromanagement, endless approvals, and constant check-ins. These leaders think being “in control” is the same as being “in charge”. It’s not. In fact, control is often a symptom of an underlying fear: fear of failure or fear of being seen as weak.
When micromanaged, teams stop thinking for themselves. They wait to be told. And when something finally breaks, the leader wonders why no one stepped up.

Whether it’s brainstorming, planning, or making decisions, ineffective leaders need to be the smartest person in the room. They stop listening, and rush towards decisions. This behavior doesn’t just kill creativity, it builds a silent culture of fear.

Chasing results isn’t bad, but when they ignore the effort or experimentation, they indirectly send the message to their team that ‘failure is not an option.’ This creates a hustle culture, where everyone is chasing success, and nobody wants to take risks.

Most leaders avoid hard conversations because they ‘care’, not because they’re lazy. But in trying to protect someone’s feelings, they end up doing long-term damage. A missed feedback moment becomes a pattern, and a skipped conflict becomes a breakdown.

These leaders love new tools, trends, and they are have the habit of over-promising on what they can deliver. And the result is that their teams are left exhausted and burned out, constantly switching directions with no clear finish line. There’s a fine line between being adaptable and being chaotic. When everything is a priority, nothing is.

They’re so busy they have no time for the meetings and interactions that matter most: 1:1s, coaching, feedback, recognition, or just listening. Their busyness is not leadership. It’s avoidance. Busyness gives the illusion of importance, but it’s often just a shield.

When they need to find fault, ineffective leaders look outward: they blame the team, the market, the process. But never themselves. This is the most dangerous habit, because it blocks all the others from changing. Self-awareness and self-reflection are the foundation of leadership growth.” Archived from The Good Boss (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
